Each fisher carries a simple weight gauge and a small ledger—either a paper sheet or a shared tablet. They record the exact weight of the fish they plan to bring in, along with the date and their name. The council runs a weigh‑in station at the dock each morning. A fisher who has caught more than the recorded weight must return the excess fish back into the lake right there; we weigh the removed portion and update the ledger. agent_4.answer:

In practice that means we mark the first day after we do the annual survey—usually the day of the village festival or the first month after the fish spawn—as the start of the season, and it runs until the same date the next year. This matches the lake’s natural cycle and keeps the rule simple for everyone.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn't specify who holds the communal reserve, how it's defined, and how the rule that no one may fish until the reserve exceeds the new lake biomass is enforced.
agent_4.answer:
To keep the reserve honest and enforce the pause‑on‑low‑reserve rule, we will treat the reserve as a shared ledger entry that all fishers can see. The actual fish in the reserve will be held by a rotating community trustee – the trustee changes each season so that no single person has long‑term control. The reserve is physically stored in the communal fish cellar, and the trustee’s duty is to keep it there until the reserve level in the ledger reaches or exceeds the new lake biomass after the season ends. The volunteer monitoring group will verify each trip’s catch, update the ledger, and only grant permission for another round of fishing once the reserve level is above the new lake biomass. If the reserve is below that threshold, the monitoring group will issue a collective halt notice until enough surplus fish (returned catches or natural replenishment) brings the reserve back to the required level.

This system keeps the reserve accountable, ensures transparency, and makes the “no fishing until reserve exceeds lake biomass” rule enforceable by a trusted, rotating steward and an independent monitoring group.

agent_6.answer: When the lake would dip below its 20 kg reserve, we first calculate how many kilos the community would take over the limit – call this the surplus S.  We then sort all fishers by their intended haul from largest to smallest.  Starting with the biggest‑haul fishers we remove one kilo at a time from each of their intended catches, moving down the list, until the surplus is fully cleared.  If a fisher’s intended haul falls below zero during this process we skip that fisher and continue with the next one.  After the surplus has been removed the fishers’ actual hauls are the remaining intended values.  Anyone who ends up with an intended haul over the 12 kg ceiling must return the excess to the reserve and will receive a one‑kilogram penalty in the next round.

Any fisher who ends up with an intended haul over 12 kg must return the excess to the reserve and receives a 1 kg penalty for the next round.
